name: Middle cerebral artery
func: The largest branch of the internal carotid artery. It supplies the outer side of each brain hemisphere, including the areas for movement and feeling in the face and arm, and, on the dominant side, language.

levels.kid:
Inside your head, your brain gets blood from a set of tubes. The biggest one on each side is the **middle cerebral artery**.

It runs out sideways along a deep fold in the brain, then spreads its branches all over the outside of the brain, like the branches of a tree covering a hill.

The parts it feeds help you move your face and arms, feel things you touch, hear, and, for most people on the left side, talk and understand words. That's why doctors are extra careful with this artery: if it gets blocked, a person might suddenly have trouble moving one arm or speaking.
levels.hs:
The **middle cerebral artery (MCA)** is the larger of the two final branches of the **internal carotid artery** (the other is the anterior cerebral artery). It starts at the base of the brain, just beside the **optic chiasm**, and runs sideways into the **lateral (Sylvian) fissure**, the deep groove that separates the frontal and parietal lobes above from the temporal lobe below. Deep in that fissure it fans out over a hidden lobe called the **insula**, then its branches climb out onto the brain's outer surface.

It supplies most of the **lateral surface** of the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes. That includes:

The **primary motor and sensory cortex** for the **face and arm** (the leg area, on the inner surface, belongs to the anterior cerebral artery).

The **language areas** (**Broca's** for speaking, **Wernicke's** for understanding) in the dominant hemisphere, usually the left.

The **auditory cortex** and parts of the visual pathways.

Tiny branches called **lenticulostriate arteries** dive straight up into deep brain structures, the **basal ganglia** and the **internal capsule**, which carries movement pathways from the cortex down to the body.
levels.college:
Neurosurgeons divide the MCA into segments. **M1** (sphenoidal/horizontal) runs from the ICA bifurcation laterally to the **limen insulae**, giving the **lenticulostriate** perforators. At or near the end of M1 it usually splits (**bifurcation**, sometimes trifurcation) into superior and inferior divisions. **M2** (insular) segments run over the insula; **M3** (opercular) segments loop around the inner faces of the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula; **M4** (cortical) branches spread over the surface.

The **superior division** typically supplies the lateral frontal lobe including Broca's area and the face/arm motor cortex; the **inferior division** supplies the lateral temporal lobe and inferior parietal lobule including **Wernicke's area**.

The lenticulostriate arteries supply the **putamen**, part of the **globus pallidus**, the **caudate head/body** and the **posterior limb of the internal capsule** region (shared with the anterior choroidal artery). They're **end arteries** without collaterals.

At the cortical surface, MCA branches form **leptomeningeal (pial) collaterals** with branches of the anterior and posterior cerebral arteries. These collaterals keep tissue alive during MCA blockage, and their quality varies hugely between people, partly explaining why some strokes are much bigger than others. The areas between the territories are the **watershed zones**, vulnerable when blood pressure falls.
levels.phd:
When an MCA is blocked, tissue forms two zones. The **core** has blood flow too low to maintain ion pumps: ATP fails, Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase stops, cells depolarize and swell (cytotoxic edema), and glutamate floods the space, causing **excitotoxicity** through NMDA receptor–driven calcium overload, activation of proteases, lipases and nitric oxide synthase, and mitochondrial injury. Around it lies the **ischemic penumbra**: electrically silent but structurally viable tissue, with flow in roughly the 10–20 mL/100 g/min range (versus about 50 normally), salvageable if flow returns.

The penumbra shrinks over time through **spreading depolarizations**, waves of depolarization that travel through injured cortex and increase metabolic demand. Inflammation follows: microglial activation, neutrophil entry and blood–brain barrier breakdown via **MMP-9**, contributing to vasogenic edema and hemorrhagic transformation.

Modern imaging measures this biology directly. **CT perfusion** and **diffusion–perfusion MRI** distinguish core (diffusion restriction, very low blood volume) from penumbra (delayed perfusion), the basis of trials (DAWN, DEFUSE-3) showing that **thrombectomy works up to 24 hours** in selected patients with "slow progressor" collaterals.

The lenticulostriate arteries, branching at right angles from a high-pressure trunk, are prone to **lipohyalinosis** and **Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms** under chronic hypertension, the classic substrate of **putaminal hemorrhage** and lacunar strokes.

Neuroprotective drugs have repeatedly failed in human trials despite animal success, a major translational puzzle; reperfusion remains the only proven strategy.
levels.expert:
**MCA stroke** gives **contralateral weakness and sensory loss of the face and arm more than the leg**, a **contralateral homonymous hemianopia** and **gaze deviation toward the lesion**. A dominant-hemisphere stroke adds **aphasia** (Broca's: halting, effortful speech; Wernicke's: fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension). Non-dominant strokes cause **hemineglect** and **anosognosia** (unawareness of the deficit).

Imaging signs: the **hyperdense MCA sign** on non-contrast CT (clot in the artery), loss of the **insular ribbon**, and blurring of the lentiform nucleus; the **ASPECTS** score grades early ischemic change in MCA territory on CT. **CT angiography** confirms large-vessel occlusion.

**Malignant MCA infarction**: a complete MCA territory infarct swells over 2–5 days and can cause herniation and death. **Decompressive hemicraniectomy** (removing a large piece of skull and opening the dura so the brain can swell outward) markedly reduces death in selected patients, a classic neurosurgical intervention.

**MCA bifurcation aneurysms** are among the most common intracranial aneurysms; rupture causes **subarachnoid hemorrhage**, often with a temporal lobe hematoma. MCA aneurysms are often treated by **microsurgical clipping** through a **pterional craniotomy** (splitting the Sylvian fissure), because their wide necks and branching make coiling harder. The MCA is also at risk in surgery for **insular gliomas** and in moyamoya disease, where **bypass** (superficial temporal artery to MCA) restores flow.

Treatment in general terms: clot-busting therapy within the time window and **mechanical thrombectomy** for large-vessel occlusion.

keyPoints: Larger terminal branch of the internal carotid; runs in the Sylvian fissure
Supplies the lateral hemisphere: face/arm motor and sensory, language
Lenticulostriate branches feed the basal ganglia and internal capsule
Stroke: contralateral face/arm weakness, aphasia (dominant), neglect (non-dominant)
Malignant MCA infarct may need decompressive hemicraniectomy

test.q: An MCA stroke typically weakens which areas most on the opposite side?
choices: Face and arm more than leg
test.explain: The leg area is on the medial surface, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery.

test.q: The MCA runs in which deep fissure of the brain?
test.explain: The lateral (Sylvian) fissure separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes.

test.q: The small deep branches of the MCA supplying the basal ganglia are the:
test.explain: Lenticulostriates arise from M1 and are end arteries; they're prone to hypertensive hemorrhage.

test.q: A left MCA stroke in a right-handed person most likely causes:
test.explain: The left hemisphere is usually dominant for language.

test.q: Removing part of the skull so a swollen infarct can expand is a decompressive ______.
test.explain: It lowers intracranial pressure and reduces death after malignant MCA infarction.

test.q: The hyperdense MCA sign on CT represents:
test.explain: Fresh thrombus is denser than flowing blood on non-contrast CT.
